newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Food low, disease risk high for Colombian refugees.
newsitem.headline: Food low, disease risk high for Colombian refugees.

text.p: Thousands of refugees camped out in this village in the jungles of northwest Colombia are battling against illness and chronic food shortages, a Red Cross aid worker said Wednesday.

More than 4,000 people huddle under hastily made plastic shelters or sleep in the open air, scared to return to their homes in the Rio Salaqui basin of neighbouring Choco province because of threats from right-wing death squads and fighting between the army and leftist guerrillas.
Many are worried about the fate of as many as 1,500 relatives still believed to be making their way across rivers and along treacherous jungle tracks as they flee the battle zone.

"We're rationing food for these displaced people because of the lack of supplies. We just don't know how long the food we have will last," said Adalberto Arrieta, of the Red Cross in the regional centre of Apartado.

Diarrhoea and fever have spread like wildfire as the refugees use a nearby river for everything from cooking water to impromptu latrines. Arrieta said under such poor hygiene conditions the risk of disease such as malaria and cholera were high.
Government Interior Minister Horacio Serpa flew to this remote area of the violence-torn Uraba region on Wednesday to see first-hand the unfolding human drama.
"This is a worrying situation. We must look for ways of solving the immediate suffering of these people and create the conditions so that they can return home," he said.

But he offered few concrete solutions to improve paltry rations of rice, plantain and yucca let alone a longer term solution to ridding their home region of illegal armed groups. So far the only international help has come from Britain with the donation of $80,000 in emergency aid, tents and food.

"What we want is for there to be no more violence in Colombia because our lives have been destroyed by fighting between the paramilitaries and the guerrilla," one teenage refugee, who did not wish to be named, said.
Despite the tough conditions in Pavarando Grande, most are prepared to face starvation and disease here than violence at home.
"It was the paramilitaries that told us to leave or face the consequences. Then the army bombardments started," said Roque Gallego, another of the refugees.

The army, however, denied it had bombed any communities and accused Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia FARC guerrillas of ordering the mass mobilisation in a bid to create "social chaos" in urban areas.
The army has waged an offensive against the guerrillas throughout the northwest Uraba region in a bid to disrupt what it claims are key arms and drug trafficking routes into and out of nearby Panama.
The guerrillas, however, say the army and the paramilitaries are waging a joint scorched earth policy to force peasants out of the strategic, resource-rich region.
More than 900,000 people have been displaced in the last decade throughout Colombia by the country's guerrilla war.
